Estintore a CO₂ (8 punti) — Jaan Kalda

Un estintore contiene CO2​ liquida in equilibrio con il suo vapore saturo a temperatura ambiente T0​=298K. Considera due casi: (a) l’estintore è tenuto capovolto, così che verso l’ugello fluisce la fase liquida; (b) è tenuto diritto, così che verso l’ugello fluisce il vapore saturo. L’ugello ha la forma di un condotto convergente–divergente (vedi figura) e il flusso al suo interno si può modellare come reversibile e adiabatico. La pressione atmosferica è patm​=1,0×105Pa; il punto triplo della CO2​ è (Tt​,pt​)=(216,6K,0,518MPa).

Qui sotto è riportato il diagramma temperatura–entropia della CO2​ con le isobare.

i) (1,5 punti) Individua la fase o le fasi presenti nel getto che esce dall’ugello e la loro temperatura.

ii) (3,5 punti) Trova la frazione in massa x di CO2​ solida nel getto in entrambi i casi.

iii) (3 punti) Considera ora una sostanza pura qualsiasi in equilibrio con il suo vapore saturo alla temperatura T, e supponi che dall’ugello esca solo il vapore (non il liquido), subendo un’espansione adiabatica reversibile. A quale condizione sul calore latente di vaporizzazione L (per unità di massa), sul calore specifico a pressione costante del vapore cp​ e sulla temperatura T una parte del vapore che esce condensa in goccioline, anche per una caduta di pressione piccolissima? La condensazione avviene per il vapore acqueo a T=373K (L≈2260kJ⋅kg−1, cp​≈2,0kJ⋅kg−1⋅K−1)?

Risposta: ii) xa​≈0,40, xb​≈0,25; iii) condensa se L/(cp​T)>1 — sì per l’acqua (≈3,0)

Soluzione: La soluzione ufficiale completa (in inglese) è nella versione originale di questo quesito e nel PDF ufficiale.

Topic: Thermodynamics Metodi: First Law of Thermodynamics, Thermodynamic Cycle Analysis Competenze: Diagrammatic Reasoning, Physical Reasoning Objects: Gas Fonte: Testo (PDF) — p.2 · Soluzione ufficiale (PDF)

Ball magnet (10 points) — Jaan Kalda

Experimental problem. Tools: ball-shaped neodymium magnet of diameter d=10mm with remanence Br​=1.2T, density ρM​≈7500kg⋅m−3; stand; permanent marker; ruler; measuring tape; flat iron disk; square wooden plate with an iron pin inserted at one side; flat wooden plate with guiding rails and non-slipping surface between them; piece of titanium of diameter 2.4mm and length 3.4mm fixed to a string. Density of titanium ρTi​≈4500kg⋅m−3.

A uniformly magnetised sphere produces an external field identical to that of a point magnetic dipole with a moment μ=34​πR3Br​/μ0​, where R is the sphere’s radius. Along the axis of a dipole, B=μ0​μ​/(2πr3), where r is the distance from the dipole. The dipole moment of the Earth is pointing southwards.

Warning: measure as far as possible from iron objects (table frames, chairs), which strongly perturb the geomagnetic field.

i) (2 points) Find the direction of the magnetisation of the magnet: mark on its surface a dot at the point where the straight magnetic field line exits, and a cross where it enters. Before leaving the room, give the magnet with the markings to the invigilator.

ii) (4 points) Find the magnitude of the Earth’s magnetic field ∣BE​∣ at the laboratory location.

iii) (4 points) Titanium is a paramagnetic material with magnetic susceptibility χ≪1. A small sample of volume V in an inhomogeneous field B(r) experiences a force F=21​(χV/μ0​)gradB2 (‘grad’ denotes derivative in the direction of greatest change). Find χ for the supplied titanium wire piece.

Risposta: experimental — e.g. ∣BE​∣≈51μT, χ∼10−4 (see the official solution)

Soluzione:

i) (2 points) The procedure has two stages: (1) locate the magnetic axis on the ball’s surface, and (2) determine which end is N (field exits) and which is S (field enters).

Stage 1: locate the axis. Place the ball-magnet on the flat iron disk. The magnet polarises the iron underneath, creating an attractive image-dipole. The interaction energy is minimised when the magnet’s dipole axis is perpendicular to the iron surface (so the two dipoles are aligned head-to-tail). The ball therefore rolls until its axis points straight down at the disk. With a permanent marker, mark a dot at the topmost point of the ball (where the axis exits the upper hemisphere). Then carefully invert the ball, place it on the disk again, and mark a second dot at the new topmost point. The two dots are diametrically opposite and lie on the dipole axis.

For full marking precision, the dot should be placed within ∼1 mm of the highest point of the ball; on a 10 mm ball this corresponds to better than ∼10∘ angular alignment.

Stage 2: identify which dot is N. At Tallinn’s latitude, the geomagnetic field BE​ points downward into the ground (the Earth’s dipole moment points southwards as stated, so its field lines re-enter the ground in the northern hemisphere). A free magnet self-orients with μ​magnet​∥BE​. Place the ball on the flat wooden plate (well away from iron objects). The geomagnetic torque rotates the ball until its dipole moment μ​ aligns with BE​ --- pointing downward, predominantly. The ball does not roll away: BE​ itself holds the ball in the aligned orientation, since once μ​∥BE​ the torque vanishes.

The N pole (where B exits, head of μ​) is then on the bottom of the ball, and the S pole on top. Re-mark the upward-pointing dot with a cross (×): this is the S pole where B enters. Leave the downward-pointing dot as a dot: this is the N pole where B exits.

Grading.

Method:

  • Realising that the magnet rolls so its axis is perpendicular to the iron disk 0.5 pts

  • Recognising that the geomagnetic field at Tallinn points downward into the ground 0.5 pts

  • Realising that the free magnet self-orients with μ​∥BE​, hence N points downward 0.5 pts

Experiment:

  • Procedure to mark both poles (dot on top, invert, dot on top again, giving two diametrically opposite axis-points) 0.2 pts

  • Both dots placed within ∼1 mm of the true axis-exit points 0.1 pts

  • Correctly marking the upward-pointing dot as a cross (S, field enters) and leaving the downward dot (N, field exits) 0.2 pts

ii) (4 points) Idea. Place the ball-magnet between the rails on the wooden plate. As the plate is tilted, gravity tries to roll the ball downhill (rotating μ​ away from BE​), while BE​ exerts a restoring magnetic torque trying to keep μ​ aligned. At a critical tilt βc​, gravity overcomes the maximum magnetic restoring torque, and the ball begins to roll. Measuring βc​ gives BE​.

Setup. The cross on the ball is slightly displaced from the exact top because BE​ is tilted from vertical (dip angle ∼70∘ in Tallinn, so the horizontal component of BE​ is non-zero and points magnetic-north). Orient the plate so that the cross’s small horizontal offset from the topmost point lies parallel to the rails. Equivalently, the rails should run along the magnetic meridian, with the ball’s dipole axis lying in the vertical plane containing BE​ and the rolling direction.

Procedure.

  • Place the plate horizontally and let the ball settle: it self-orients with μ​∥BE​, with the cross slightly offset toward magnetic-south of the topmost point.

  • Re-orient the plate (in the horizontal plane) so the cross’s offset is parallel to the rails (cross equidistant from both rails).

  • Slowly tilt one end of the plate upward. Measure the elevation h of the higher end above the lower end with the ruler; for a plate of length L, the tilt angle satisfies sinβ=h/L.

  • Continue tilting smoothly and slowly until the ball just begins to roll down. Record h at that instant.

  • Lower the plate, slightly displace the ball to reset, allow re-orientation, repeat. Average over many trials --- readings fluctuate due to small variations in initial alignment, friction at the rails, and the smoothness of tilting.

Force/torque balance. Just before rolling, the ball is in static equilibrium between gravity and the magnetic restoring torque. The gravitational torque about the ball’s center (acting through the rail contact at distance r) is τg​=mgrsinβ, where r=d/2 is the ball radius. The maximum magnetic restoring torque (when μ​⊥BE​) is τmag,max​=μBE​. Critical condition: μBE​=mgrsinβc​, BE​=μmgrsinβc​​​.

The magnet’s dipole moment is μ=(4πr3/3)Br​/μ0​=0.50A⋅m2, with mass m=ρM​⋅(4πr3/3)≈3.93g. So μmgr​=0.503.93×10−3⋅9.8⋅0.005​≈385μT.

Measurements. A representative set of trials with rail length L=19cm:

trial12345678910avg
h (mm)2426252723252624252525.0

The standard deviation of the readings is σh​≈0.12cm, giving a standard error on the mean of σh​/10​≈0.04cm, or about 1.5% of the average.

With sinβc​=hˉ/L=0.025/0.19≈0.132: BE​=μmgrsinβc​​=385μT⋅0.132≈51μT.

Combined uncertainty (statistical from σh​ plus systematic from μ and r at the few-percent level): BE​≈51(3)μT, in good agreement with the known geomagnetic field at Tallinn’s latitude (∼50 μT).

Grading.

  • Recognising that gravity drives rolling and magnetic torque resists it 0.2 pts

  • Gravity torque on ball: τg​=mgrsinβ (force times lever arm r to contact line) 0.2 pts

  • Maximum magnetic torque τmag,max​=μBE​ (when μ​⊥BE​) 0.3 pts

  • Procedure: tilt the plate and record the critical angle when the ball begins to roll 0.4 pts

  • Realising that the rails should be aligned with the cross’s horizontal offset (i.e., parallel to the magnetic meridian) 0.4 pts

  • Critical-condition formula μBE​=mgrsinβc​ 0.5 pts

  • Solving for BE​=mgrsinβc​/μ 0.3 pts

  • Computing μ=(4πr3/3)Br​/μ0​ from the given Br​ and ball geometry 0.4 pts

  • Documented measurements (multiple trials, table or list of readings) with averaging and uncertainties 0.8 pts

  • Plausible numerical answer for BE​ in the range 30μT to 70μT 0.5 pts

iii) (4 points) Setup. The titanium piece hangs as a pendulum from a string of length L attached to the stand. Bring the ball-magnet close to the Ti so that one of its poles touches the Ti’s surface. The paramagnetic Ti is attracted toward the magnet. Slowly and smoothly pull the magnet-and-Ti combination horizontally; the pendulum tilts. At a critical horizontal displacement xc​, the magnetic attraction can no longer balance the gravitational restoring force, and the Ti detaches from the magnet and swings back. Measuring xc​ gives χ.

Practical execution.

  • Keep the magnet stuck to the iron pin in the wooden plate as a holder, so it always points one pole forward (rather than rotating in the hand).

  • Ensure the magnet’s pole touches the Ti at all times and at the same point (the magnet’s tip, on the dipole axis); a slight shift up or down reduces the magnetic force.

  • Pull very slowly so the system is quasi-static (no inertial effects, a≈0).

  • Repeat many times. Take the maximum observed xc​ as the result; smaller readings reflect imperfect execution (acceleration, off-axis contact, etc.).

A typical observed range: xc​≈210mm to 260mm.

Physics. The ball-magnet has dipole moment μ=(4π/3)(d/2)3Br​/μ0​≈0.50A⋅m2. On its dipole axis, at distance r from the centre, B(r)=2πr3μ0​μ​.

At the moment of contact with the Ti, the smallest distance from the magnet’s center to the Ti’s center is rmin​=(d/2)+dTi​/2≈5+1.2=6.2mm.

The force on the paramagnetic Ti, using the formula given in the problem with B2∝1/r6 and ∣∇B2∣=6B2/r: Fmag​=21​μ0​χVTi​​⋅6rB2(r)​=4π2r73χVTi​μ0​μ2​.

Force balance at detachment. Just before the Ti detaches, the pendulum’s tilt angle θc​ satisfies sinθc​=xc​/L, and the horizontal restoring force is mTi​gtanθc​. Setting this equal to the maximum magnetic force (at r=rmin​): mTi​gtanθc​=4π2rmin7​3χVTi​μ0​μ2​.

Using mTi​=ρTi​VTi​ to cancel VTi​: χ=3μ0​μ24π2ρTi​gtanθc​⋅rmin7​​.

Numerical evaluation. Take pendulum length L=1.0m (estimated from the stand) and xc​=235mm (representative maximum from many trials). Then sinθc​=0.235, tanθc​≈0.242. With ρTi​=4500m3kg​: χ≈3⋅4π×10−7⋅0.524π2⋅4500⋅9.8⋅0.242⋅(6.2×10−3)7​≈1.6×10−4​.

This is consistent with the literature value for pure titanium (χTi​≈1.8×10−4), within the precision afforded by the experimental uncertainties.

Grading.

  • Setup: pendulum + magnet, identification of detachment as the limit condition 0.3 pts

  • Practical execution detail: keep magnet on iron pin to maintain orientation 0.2 pts

  • Practical execution detail: ensure pole touches Ti at the same axial point 0.2 pts

  • Practical execution detail: pull slowly (quasi-static, a≈0) 0.2 pts

  • Performing ≥5 measurements (either stated explicitly that the reported value is the maximum of ≥5 trials, or ≥5 measurements documented in a table/list) 0.4 pts

  • Taking the maximum (not average) of the measurements as the reported xc​ 0.4 pts

  • Combining the given dipole-field and paramagnetic-force formulas into Fmag​=3χVTi​μ0​μ2/(4π2r7) 0.3 pts

  • Identifying rmin​ as magnet radius + Ti half-thickness (accounting for the wire’s radius) 0.4 pts

  • Force balance mgtanθc​=Fmag,max​ (or equivalently sinθc​ if the magnet is pulled perpendicular to the thread rather than strictly horizontally; the two forms differ by ∼3% at the critical angle, smaller than experimental scatter; both can be approximated as θ) 0.5 pts

  • Solving this equation for χ=4π2ρTi​gtanθc​rmin7​/(3μ0​μ2) 0.3 pts

  • Documenting the observed maximum θc​. Full credit for θc​∈[11.9∘,14.5mm]; reduce by 0.1 pts per half a degree outside this range, down to a minimum of 0 0.3 pts

  • Numerical answer for χ. Full credit for χ∈[1.5×10−4,1.9×10−4]; reduce by 0.1 pts for each 0.1×10−4 outside this range, down to a minimum of 0 0.5 pts

Grading note (default credit for execution details): if the three execution details (iron-pin holder, axial pole contact, slow quasi-static pulling) are not stated explicitly but the reported maximum horizontal displacement is at least 220mm, award 50% of each item’s points (0.1 pts each, keep one decimal). The reasoning: a result in this range can only be obtained if execution was acceptable, even if the student didn’t articulate why.

Magnete sferico (10 punti) — Jaan Kalda

Problema sperimentale. Materiale: magnete sferico al neodimio di diametro d=10mm con magnetizzazione residua Br​=1,2T e densità ρM​≈7500kg⋅m−3; supporto; pennarello indelebile; righello; metro a nastro; disco di ferro piatto; tavoletta quadrata di legno con un perno di ferro inserito su un lato; tavoletta piana di legno con guide e superficie antiscivolo tra di esse; pezzetto di titanio di diametro 2,4mm e lunghezza 3,4mm fissato a un filo. Densità del titanio ρTi​≈4500kg⋅m−3.

Una sfera magnetizzata uniformemente produce all’esterno lo stesso campo di un dipolo magnetico puntiforme di momento μ=34​πR3Br​/μ0​, dove R è il raggio della sfera. Lungo l’asse di un dipolo B=μ0​μ​/(2πr3), dove r è la distanza dal dipolo. Il momento di dipolo della Terra è diretto verso sud.

Attenzione: misura il più lontano possibile da oggetti di ferro (telai dei tavoli, sedie), che perturbano fortemente il campo geomagnetico.

i) (2 punti) Trova la direzione della magnetizzazione del magnete: segna sulla sua superficie un punto dove esce la linea di campo rettilinea e una croce dove entra. Prima di lasciare l’aula consegna il magnete con i segni al sorvegliante.

ii) (4 punti) Trova il modulo del campo magnetico terrestre ∣BE​∣ nel luogo del laboratorio.

iii) (4 punti) Il titanio è un materiale paramagnetico con suscettività magnetica χ≪1. Un piccolo campione di volume V in un campo non uniforme B(r) subisce una forza F=21​(χV/μ0​)gradB2 (“grad” indica la derivata nella direzione di massima variazione). Trova χ per il pezzetto di filo di titanio fornito.

Risposta: sperimentale — ad es. ∣BE​∣≈51μT, χ∼10−4 (vedi la soluzione ufficiale)

Soluzione: La soluzione ufficiale completa (in inglese) è nella versione originale di questo quesito e nel PDF ufficiale.
